name: Branding (skin)

lead: Skin branding applies a heated metal object, electrocautery or other methods to cause a burn that heals into a permanent scar pattern. In body-art communities it is chosen for self-expression and for the raised, textured design it leaves.

It belongs to the wider family of scarification, which has long been practised in parts of Africa, Melanesia and Australia for rites of passage and identity. Medical literature mostly documents its complications.

paras: In body modification, designs are made by specialists and healing is a long process, commonly 6 to 12 months for scarification in general, with spreading scars making simple designs more common. A separate, non-aesthetic tradition uses branding as folk therapy in some countries.

Branding causes third-degree burns. Case series report infections, cellulitis and other complications, and keloid scarring can occur. Shared tools have been linked to transmission of bloodborne infections in scarification generally.

angle.text: Branding creates a permanent patterned scar that people choose as body art. The look is the scar's texture and shape, and it cannot be easily removed.

lead: Skin branding is a body-art method in which third-degree burns are inflicted with hot metal, electrocautery, laser, chemicals or freezing to produce permanent scars.[1] It is practised in many indigenous cultures and became common in western body-modification scenes.[1]

In the looksmaxxing context it is a fringe appearance modification: instead of ink, the design is the scar itself. It is separate from therapeutic branding used by folk healers for counter-irritation.[2][3]
Published literature consists mainly of case reports and series describing complications.[1][2]
infobox: Hot metal, electrocautery, laser, chemical, freezing

paras: Aesthetic branding is described in the burn literature as a form of body art in which third-degree burns produce permanent scars, performed with methods including electrocautery, laser, chemicals, freezing and hot metal. The authors of a 2006 report say it is not a manifestation of a psychiatric disorder but a method of self-expression.[1]
Scarification more broadly means cutting, scratching, etching or burning designs into skin; scars tend to spread as they heal, so final designs are usually simple and outcomes are hard to predict.[4]

Scarification is traditionally practised in parts of Africa, Melanesia and Australia and among some Indigenous cultures of the Americas, marking rites of passage, identity and sometimes medicinal treatment. Colonial governments and missionaries stigmatised and criminalised it in places.[4]
Separately, branding is used by some traditional healers, for example for jaundice in children in southern India, where it is described as a cultural dermatosis.[5]

No controlled studies of branding for appearance exist. Case literature includes a 2009 series of adverse clinical sequelae after skin branding, a 2006 report on aesthetic branding with adverse outcomes, and reports of abdominal cellulitis and of children branded for jaundice.[1][2][5][6]

Reports describe burns, infection and cellulitis.[2][6] Infection is common when tools are unsterilised, shared tools have been linked to HIV and hepatitis C transmission, and keloids may form.[4] Clinicians are advised to be aware of the practice to avoid misdiagnosis.[5]
